questions.question: How should RocketMQ 5.x message types shape topic design?
options: Mix normal, FIFO, delay, and transaction messages in one topic and separate them with tags
Declare one message type per topic and split different delivery contracts into different topics
Choose the message type independently on every consumer
Use one consumer group for each message type in the same topic
questions.explanation: RocketMQ 5.x models message type as topic metadata. Separate topics keep delivery behavior, operations, and validation explicit; tags are for filtering within a business domain.

questions.question: A workload publishes 20,000 messages/second with an average 1 KiB payload. About how much raw payload arrives in one hour before replicas, indexes, metadata, or compression?
options: About 7 GiB
About 69 GiB
About 720 GiB
About 2 TiB
questions.explanation: 20,000 x 1 KiB x 3,600 seconds is about 68.7 GiB. Provisioning still needs measured overhead, replication, filesystem behavior, and retention headroom.

questions.question: What ordering contract should an application assume for FIFO messages?
options: Every message in the RocketMQ cluster has one global order
Messages are ordered only by producer wall-clock time
Messages with the same message group are delivered in send order
All consumer groups share one processing order
questions.explanation: FIFO ordering is scoped to a message group. Use a stable entity key such as orderId, and keep independent entities in separate groups so they can make progress concurrently.

questions.question: A consumer commits a payment update, then times out before RocketMQ receives success. What should the system expect?
options: RocketMQ can inspect the payment database and mark the message complete
The message may be delivered again, so the payment handler needs a durable idempotency receipt
The message is always sent directly to the DLQ without another attempt
The original payment update is automatically rolled back
questions.explanation: The broker sees an unknown consumption result and may redeliver. Commit a stable event receipt with the payment mutation so a replay returns the first result instead of charging again.

questions.question: What does a RocketMQ dead-letter queue accomplish?
options: It permanently fixes invalid payloads
It proves the consumer side effect happened exactly once
It isolates messages that exceeded the retry policy so healthy work can continue
It replaces monitoring and replay runbooks
questions.explanation: A DLQ is quarantine after retries are exhausted. Operators still need to diagnose the cause, repair the payload or code, and replay safely with the original event identity.

questions.question: When is SimpleConsumer a better fit than PushConsumer?
options: When the application needs explicit receive and acknowledgement control with a managed invisibility duration
When every handler is short, synchronous, and should use SDK-managed concurrency
When consumer retries must be disabled globally
When several consumer APIs must be mixed in one consumer group
questions.explanation: SimpleConsumer exposes atomic receive and acknowledgement operations and lets the application manage processing duration. PushConsumer is simpler for predictable synchronous listener work.
